newsitem.title: GERMANY: Japan declares at G7 that yen's fall is complete.
newsitem.headline: Japan declares at G7 that yen's fall is complete.

text.p: Japan declared at the Group of Seven (G7) meeting here on Saturday that the yen's downward correction is completely over but left the question of whether Tokyo is ready to back up those words with deeds unanswered.
The G7, in an unusual move, issued a statement on currencies saying that major misalignments in exchange markets noted in its April 1995 communique have been corrected.
"In other words, the statement made clear that the yen's downward correction process has been completely over," said Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka.
Mitsuzuka said he was "quite satisfied" with the outcome of the G7 meeting, which was in line with Japan's policy stance towards foreign exchange markets.
Japanese officials have been saying that excessive currency volatility is not desirable, and currencies should reflect fundamentals.
But, despite the strong statement, the world's richest economies did not reach an agreement on concerted foreign exchange intervention or even talk about it.
German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said financial leaders from the G7 did not discuss using intervention in world currency markets at a meeting.

Asked about the possibility the Bank of Japan would intervene to sell dollars, possibly with other central banks, if the yen slid further in post-G7 markets, Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance (MOF) International Finance Bureau said "we will cooperate, as being said in the statement."
He did not elaborate but added the G7 wanted to send a clear message to the market and thus, issued the statement.
The G7 also said in the statement that they would monitor developments in foreign exchange markets and to cooperate, as appropriate.
But, even without help from other G7 central banks, Japan has plenty of ammunition to defend the yen if they want to and if the situation allows.
Japan has the world's largest external reserves, tallying $217.136 billion at the end of January.
The yen has been hardest hit by the dollar's recent strength, with the dollar gaining more than 50 percent against the yen since its all-time low of 79.75 yen in April, 1995.
Japanese officials have expressed displeasure over the yen's recent steep decline, which could lead Japan's trade surplus to balloon again and further damange Tokyo stock prices.

But so far, Japan has steered clear of intervening with dollar sales, partly due to fears any attempt to achieve even a mild dollar drop runs the risk of setting the market off on a relentless yen decline and causing an unintended chain reaction that would disrupt the balance in world financial markets.
In addition, Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita said the "yen's depreciation since the beginning of this year has been rather rapid and the pace of import price increase has been accelerating."
Matsushita said he hopes currencies will stabilise now in response to the G7 agreement on currencies.

Matsushita also denounced notions that Japan's extremely easy credit policy has been one cause behind the yen's recent fall. Japan's official discount rate has sat at a record low 0.5 percent since September, 1995.
"You cannot link the easy monetary policy, which has been in place over the last two years, for the recent weakening of the yen," Matsushita said after the Berlin meeting.
Japan's monetary policy takes a lot of factors into consideration, not just currency market developments, he said.
